purpose: Cisplatin is a powerful chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including testicular, ovarian, and bladder cancers. It can be used alone or combined with other cancer treatments. Your doctor has chosen it because it is very effective at fighting certain cancer cells.
how_it_works: Cisplatin works by getting inside cancer cells and attaching itself to their DNA, which is like the cell's instruction manual. Once it damages the DNA, the cancer cell can no longer grow or copy itself and eventually dies. Healthy cells can sometimes repair this damage, but cancer cells usually cannot, which is what makes cisplatin effective.
common_side_effects: Nausea and vomiting are very common, though your care team will give you medicines to help control this. You may also notice kidney strain, hearing changes or ringing in the ears, numbness or tingling in your hands and feet, hair loss, low blood cell counts (which can increase infection risk or cause fatigue), and appetite loss.
warnings: Cisplatin can seriously damage your kidneys, so you will receive plenty of IV fluids before and after treatment to protect them. It can also cause permanent hearing loss, especially at high doses — your hearing may be checked regularly. It can lower your blood counts, raising your risk of infections, bleeding, and anemia. Tell your doctor right away if you feel feverish, notice unusual bruising or bleeding, or experience significant changes in urination. This medicine can harm an unborn baby, so reliable birth control is very important during treatment.
typical_dosing: Cisplatin is given through an IV (directly into a vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting — you will not take it as a pill at home. The dose depends on your body size, the type of cancer being treated, and whether it is combined with other medicines. It is commonly given once every 3 to 4 weeks, or sometimes weekly at a lower dose. Your oncology team will determine the exact schedule that is right for you.
